blocks.p: Between the two bundles of washi in the bottom drawer there was a third sheet, and it was the colour of rust.

Rei lifted it out by the edges. He knew what it was before he had it in the light, because he had read the page the morning before and had hoped, the way a person hopes about a lump, that he would never see one. A self closed and struck through. A mouth sealed, and the thing inside it burned. A door drawn shut over the body, ringed in locks. The most complex figure in Gin's book, drawn here in a brown that had once been red, by a hand that had not leaned yet.
It was finished except for one stroke. The last one. The one a person makes himself, over his own heart.

I have drawn it correctly twice, both times for others who asked, both times burned unused. There was no name on this one. There did not need to be. Gin had drawn it for himself, sometime in the last good weeks, when something had started thinning the wall toward him and he had felt watched and blamed the wrong thing. He had drawn it the way he drew everything, in advance, carefully, so it would be there if he needed it. Then he had put it in the drawer beside the circle that could save him, and gone to work, and come home one Wednesday too tired to know he was tired.
Let it be me, he had said at the rail. I am already most of the way gone.

Rei stood at the sink with the sheet in one hand and the lighter in the other for a long time. The lighter was the cheap one he had carried for years and turned over in his fingers whenever he was waiting for something, and he only noticed now that he had been turning it all afternoon. Then he burned the Final Refusal over the drain and watched the brown figure curl and go. Gin had drawn it twice for others and both times it had burned unused. Rei made it three.

He packed Gin's field kit on the kitchen table, the way Gin had packed it in front of him a hundred times while he pretended to watch television. It looked like the kit of a man going camping. That was the point.

Threshold wards, folded into strips, into the left front pocket, where Gin had kept them in every bag he owned. Three sealed vials of sulphur, small glass, intact, left side. Six prepared configurations from the desk, each in its own sleeve, each labelled in Gin's small print. He counted them twice and stopped at nine prepared glyphs in total, because Gin had written that more than ten could be felt by anyone reading. Into the inside pocket of his jacket went the two washi bundles with the compass roses on them, the exorcism circle in five parts, sealed separately, two complete sets. Gin had used one set once in six years, after three months of preparation. Rei had had an afternoon.

He could not draw a single one of them. He had understood that reading the chapter. Gin's post-it said it plainly. Studying this gives understanding. It does not give the hand. But the hand had already been given, by Gin, on a Monday morning with forty sheets of Kanda washi on the desk. I prepared more than I will use. I do not know why I did that today specifically. Rei thought he knew now. Part of Gin had been packing for this night before either of them knew it would come.
Last, because his hands would not do it any sooner, he took the folded Stability Mark out of his shirt pocket and looked at the R. in the corner, and put it back over his heart.

He was sitting in the genkan with his shoes on when he remembered the page he had always skipped. It was near the end of the book, headed in Gin's tidy print, and he had skipped it the first time because it had looked like a list of types, the kind of thing a recruitment office would print.

doc.title: Gin's book. The Eight Patterns. How people come to this work
lines: A Saturday. Rei is playing video games. I am writing about the eight ways a person can begin to understand what they are, because no two practitioners find the veil through the same door.
Entry point is not class. It is starting position.
One. The Registered Practitioner. Official, inside the system. Access and surveillance in equal measure. Kato is Entry One. Adachi is Entry One.
Two. The Grid Operative. Unregistered. Network trust. Tanizaki is Entry Two. He has been Grid since before I was born.
Three. The Civilian Medium. Sensitive, unframed. The world just became very large.
Four. The Suppressed. Hiding what they are. Real rank at least two levels above what they show. The performance is the protection. This is the one I know best. I am aware that I am describing myself.
Five. The Institutional Enforcer. The system's instrument. Interesting when the system asks for the wrong thing.
Six. The Possessed. A good spirit sharing your body with your full awareness and consent.
Seven. The Witness. Zero rank or near it. Survives by being the person no one sees coming.
Eight. The Demon. A demon in a Vessel Program body, under formal contract with the CVD. You remember being human.
Rei is Entry Four. He does not know this yet. He will. Documentation is not exposure. It is care. G.U. A Sunday. Rei is in the next room.

blocks.p: Rei read the last line and laughed once, out loud, in the empty genkan, because it was so exactly like Gin to write a thing like that and then go and make dinner. He had been in the next room. He could almost remember the Sunday. He had been annoyed about something. He had no idea, then, that he was being written down with love.

Entry Four. Hiding what they are. The performance is the protection. For six years he had performed being nothing much, a crime-scene temp with bad sleep and a headache habit, because his brother had taught him to, at a kitchen table, as a trick for sleeping. Tonight, at the river, the performance would end. Whatever he was, he would be it in front of everything.

He thought about what the Healer had shown him all month without ever saying it. There were two ways to grow into a seat. The grain the far shore had left in his palms was hungry. He could feel it. It wanted other registers the way a mouth wants bread, and if he fed it, if he took in other people's feeling to grow fast, he would get strong very quickly. That was what a Qliphoth did. It ate a holder out from under a seat and wore the register as a hollow shell. The other way was the way the twelve did it. Hold one register open and steady with one's own self, sane and willing, every morning, for as long as it took. It was slower. It was the only clean one.
He closed his fists over the grain and did not feed it.
In the genkan with his shoes on and three folded pages over his heart, the whole night stopped being an idea and became a fact in his body, which is the only place ideas ever finally land.

He could not be at the seam and at the chair and at his brother's side at the same hour, because by the cruelty of how this had been built they were the same hour, and a body is one body in one place. Even a body that can feel both sides of a wall. To put his hand on the wall was to take it off the chair. To reach for his brother was to leave the wall unread at the moment it could be written on. There was no arrangement of the night in which all his hands were where he wanted them. The month-long dread he had not been able to name was only that. A simple animal fact, wearing the costume of complexity, because complexity is bearable and a single forced step is not.

He thought about the twelve. Each of them must have stood once in a genkan like this, with their own pages folded over their own hearts, and gone out, and become what going out made them. Watanabe weakening. Mori Takao at his boiler for forty years. Park Junho on his knees. None of them had got to hold every clock. That was what a seat cost, and what a wall cost, and, Rei understood now, what a brother cost. Not the price paid at the river, which would be loud and quick. This. The doors that close softly behind a person as he walks out of a flat, the ones he never gets to find out were the right ones.

The drums were louder now. The grey outside had gone to the particular blue that meant the festival's last night had begun. Up and down the ward people were carrying the small fires out to their doorsteps to send their dead home. Somewhere along the embankment his brother was already standing at the rail in his grey cardigan, looking at a doubled river, glad in two ways at once that Rei was coming.

Rei put his hand on the door. He did not feel ready. He had stopped believing readiness had ever been on the table. He felt, instead, the thing Higuchi's smallest letters had really been about. Not fear of the wall. The terrible privilege of being the one person who can feel both sides of a closing door, and has to decide anyway which side to be on when it shuts.

He heard his own door click shut behind him, and the sound was smaller than the thing it was, the way the important sounds always are. That was the real foreclosure. Not the river. This small click. The flat with its three pages no longer laid out, the version of the night where he stayed in the grey hour reading and never had to go, sealed away behind the sound a key makes.
He went down through the shut streets toward the water, and the ward came out to meet him.

blocks.cap: The dead market arcade, shutters down

blocks.p: He passed the dead market arcade two streets north of the market, its shutters down, its storm drains breathing cold air in August. Gin's book called it a crossing point and said never stand over one you have not warded. Rei walked in the middle of the road. Above the arcade, in a cheap flat, one window was lit. A man in a vest sat at it with his head in his hands, the posture of someone who has been tired for a year and thinks it is age. On the sill beside him a row of potted plants had died, all of them, but only on the side of the room nearest the arcade. The nameplate by the street door said Tachibana. Rei stopped dead on the tarmac. Then he made himself breathe. It was a common name. It was not the same man. It was only a tired stranger being slowly drunk by the arcade underneath him, and Rei had no hour to give him tonight. He filed the window with the others.

He passed under the third railway arch, where a door with no handle stood in the brick and a bartender with a cigarette, Goro, leaned beside it watching the festival go by. Goro looked at Rei's face and then at the kit bag and lifted two fingers from his cigarette in a kind of salute. He did not say anything. At Kemuri, nobody ever did.

blocks.cap: Nagai Haruto at the north bridge

blocks.p: At the north bridge a knot of kids sat on the concrete steps above the water with cans and phones, loud, too close to the edge. A boy of seventeen with a faded brown inch at the ends of his black hair stood a little apart from them with his hands in his pockets, turning something in one of them. A river stone. Nagai Haruto. Rei knew the name from the ward's talk about the riverside kids. He was the one the others listened to. As Rei watched, the boy glanced at a patch of water just downstream, as if someone had spoken from it, and then stepped between two of the others a second before one of them would have shoved the other in. The water was quieter where he stood. Rei, with his registers half up, saw what stood in it with him. A small boy, wet to the shoulders, keeping watch on the same stretch of river, so that no third child would join him.

blocks.cap: The drowned boy who keeps watch beside him

blocks.p: Rei kept walking. He promised the two of them, silently, that he would come back.

Below the embankment, at the riverside memorial, the old woman in the flowered apron was setting out her lanterns. Okuma Sumi. Rei had heard her name from Choi Hana, who read grief for a living and said she worried about the memorial keeper and did not know what to do. Mrs. Okuma was frailer than she had been even the night before. She was setting out an extra lantern, the one she kept for the bad anniversaries. The memorial was warmer with her there. Rei could feel the grief of the March ground leaning toward her the way the lanterns leaned toward the far bank, drinking gently.

"You'll want to hurry," she said without looking up. "The river's going a long way tonight. I've a mind to go with it one of these years. I gave my good umbrella to the girl next door this afternoon. She'll get more use of it."
Rei stopped. He did not have time. He stopped anyway.
"Will you be here tomorrow night?" he asked. "And the night after? My brother's going to need someone to light one for him. I don't know how. I've never done it right."
She looked up at him then, properly, with wet kind eyes. For a moment the warmth around her seemed to hesitate.
"Somebody has to show you, then," she said slowly. "Don't they."
"Somebody has to," Rei said.

Ahead of him the river was doing what Higuchi's most frightened letters had promised. Two banks where there should be one. Two cities a degree out of true. The seam between them bright and soft and thinning toward the hour all three of his clocks had been falling toward since the year the lights went grey.

He stopped once, at the turn of the path where he could see his brother. The grey cardigan. The rail. The two kinds of gladness already turning toward the sound of his shoes on the gravel. And across the river, on the far embankment, not Kaito this time. A woman in her late thirties in a pale cardigan, a few greys left in her hair on purpose, standing very straight with her hands folded, and behind her, coming up the far steps in a slow silent line, thirty or more people in mourning clothes. Kanna-sensei had come herself.
Rei let his two suppressed registers come all the way up for the first time in a month. Both sides at once. No half measure, because half measures are for reading, and he was done reading.

The city went double and bright and unbearable and beautiful around him. The lanterns and their held-breath shadows. The wall and its soft thin wound. The brother and the Healer in one body. The thing in Fukai Rinka's body, smiling across the water with a dead woman's gentle face. And at the centre of it all, very far down, a tired man in an old coat with his back to the world, holding a door.
The three clocks touched the same hour. Rei stepped onto the embankment.
